premises.content:
A compact multi-orbital tight-binding Hamiltonian for a GeS monolayer is formulated on an orthogonal basis containing the $3s$ and $3p_{x,y,z}$ orbitals of each Ge and S atom, with four atoms per unit cell and a resulting $16\times16$ matrix Hamiltonian,
      $$
      H \;=\; \sum_{i}\sum_{\alpha}\left[ \varepsilon_{\alpha}^{i}\, c_{\alpha}^{i\dagger} c_{\alpha}^{i} \;+\; \sum_{j}\sum_{\beta} t_{\alpha\beta}^{(j)}\, c_{\alpha}^{i\dagger} c_{\beta}^{j} \right] \;+\; \mathrm{h.c.},
      $$
      where $i,j$ label atomic sites, $\alpha,\beta\in\{s,p_x,p_y,p_z\}$ label orbital degrees of freedom, $\varepsilon_{\alpha}^{i}$ are on-site orbital energies, and $t_{\alpha\beta}^{(j)}$ are inter-atomic hopping matrix elements given by the Slater--Koster relations
      $$
      \begin{aligned}
      t_{ss} &= V_{ss\sigma}(d),\\[4pt]
      t_{s\alpha} &= \dfrac{d^{\alpha}}{d}\, V_{sp\sigma}(d),\\[6pt]
      t_{\alpha\beta} &= \dfrac{d^{\alpha}d^{\beta}}{d^{2}}\, V_{pp\sigma}(d)
         \;+\; \left(\delta_{\alpha\beta}-\dfrac{d^{\alpha}d^{\beta}}{d^{2}}\right) V_{pp\pi}(d),
      \end{aligned}
      $$
      with $\boldsymbol{d}=(d^{x},d^{y},d^{z})$ the inter-atomic displacement vector and $d=|\boldsymbol{d}|$. The distance dependence of each transfer integral $V_{lmn}(d)$, with orbital types $l,m\in\{s,p\}$ and bond character $n\in\{\sigma,\pi\}$, is parameterized by
      $$
      V_{lmn}(d) \;=\; \eta_{lmn}\,\dfrac{\hbar^{2}}{m_{e}}\;\exp\!\left[-\lambda_{lmn}\!\left(\dfrac{d}{\Delta}-1\right)\right],
      $$
      where $\eta_{lmn}$ and $\lambda_{lmn}$ are dimensionless bond-type coefficients, $\Delta$ is a reference length in \AA{} chosen for each bond type, $\hbar$ is the reduced Planck constant, $m_{e}$ is the electron mass, and the model includes $s$--$p$ mixing through the $t_{s\alpha}$ terms while retaining hoppings up to the eight lattice displacement vectors enumerated for the GeS unit cell.

No load-bearing weak point was identified beyond routine model-completeness concerns, and the result is best read as a solid formulation of the intended GeS tight-binding basis rather than a claim that has been independently validated against a separate benchmark.", "keywords": ["16\u00d716 Hamiltonian", "Slater\u2013Koster", "distance-dependent hoppings"], "structural_edges": [{"target": "paper:812798606909112322::conclusion_2", "type": "supports"}]}

steps.reasoning: Starting from the tight-binding Hamiltonian form and the distance-law parametrization $V_{l m n}(d)=\eta_{l m n} \dfrac{\hbar^{2}}{m_{e}} \exp\!\left[-\lambda_{l m n}\!\left(\dfrac{d}{\Delta}-1\right)\right]$ (the model established above), the authors treat the bond-type coefficients $\eta_{l m n}$, $\lambda_{l m n}$ and the reference length $\Delta$ (for each bond type Ge→S, Ge→Ge and S→S) as adjustable parameters to be determined by fitting to first-principles band energies.

To quantify the fit between tight-binding eigenvalues and first-principles band energies, define the weighted chi-squared objective function
$
\chi^{2}=\sum_{i=C, V} \sum_{j=1}^{N} \sigma_{j}^{2}\left[E_{i}^{T B}(j)-E_{i}^{D F T}(j)\right]^{2},
$
where the outer sum $i\in\{C,V\}$ runs over conduction-band ($C$) and valence-band ($V$) states considered in the fit, the inner sum index $j=1\ldots N$ enumerates the $N$ sampled $k$-points and/or band indices included in the comparison, $\sigma_{j}$ is a weight assigned to data point $j$, $E_{i}^{T B}(j)$ is the tight-binding energy for band $i$ at point $j$, and $E_{i}^{D F T}(j)$ is the reference DFT (HSE06) energy for the same band and point. The authors state that $\chi^{2}$ is evaluated as a sum of weighted squared residuals and cite prior use of such a procedure.
[12]

The numerical search for optimal parameters was performed by generating a large pool of candidate parameter sets (the authors report generating 10000 parameter sets) and selecting the set that minimizes the $\chi^{2}$ objective; the authors describe this as an optimisation procedure and elsewhere indicate the use of a Genetic algorithm for the transfer-integral optimization process, thereby combining systematic parameter sampling with a selection criterion that directly targets agreement with the DFT band energies.
[10]

The outcome of the minimization is reported as a compact numerical parameter set (values of $\eta_{lmn}$, $\lambda_{lmn}$ and $\Delta$ for each of the three bond types Ge→S, Ge→Ge and S→S). These optimized numerical values are presented in the paper in a tabulated form (Table 2) and are the parameter values used subsequently to generate the tight-binding band dispersions and orbital projections.

motivating_questions.content: To convert the TB Hamiltonian into a predictive, transferable model one must supply quantitative transfer-integral parameters that control the strength and range of $ss$, $sp$ and $pp$ hoppings for each bond type. Prior TB efforts lacked a compact, systematically fitted parameter set referenced to high-accuracy DFT (HSE06) for GeS, which left TB predictions qualitatively uncertain when used for anisotropy-sensitive properties. A small, physically interpretable parameter set per bond-type ($\eta_{lmn},\lambda_{lmn},\Delta$) fitted to DFT eigenvalues is therefore necessary to make the TB model quantitatively accurate while retaining computational simplicity for larger-scale calculations.

The tight-binding parameters are fitted to LDA total energies and band structures for bulk oxides. LDA is known to underestimate band gaps and can incorrectly treat strongly correlated d- and f-electrons in transition-metal oxides. For rutile TiO2, LDA gives an indirect gap of about 1.8 eV while the experimental gap is 3.0 eV. This discrepancy can affect surface states and relaxation, especially if charge transfer and polarization at surfaces are involved.
      P. K. Schelling, J. W. Halley, and N. Yu, Phys. Rev. B58, 1279 (1998).

steps.reasoning: State the tight-binding (TB) modelling ingredients and the role of overlap and transfer parameters. In the TB approximation, initial Bloch states are written as linear combinations of localized atomic orbitals with coefficients $C_{ij}(\mathbf{k})$. The TB secular equation involves an overlap matrix $\mathcal{S}(\mathbf{k})$ and a transfer (Hamiltonian) matrix $\mathcal{H}(\mathbf{k})$, whose off-diagonal elements (e.g. the nearest-neighbour overlap parameter $s$ and hopping parameter $t$) are conventionally chosen to reproduce the empirical or desired band structure of graphene. These parameters enter the generalized eigenvalue problem $\left[\mathcal{H}-E_i(\mathbf{k})\mathcal{S}\right]\cdot \mathbf{C}_i(\mathbf{k})=0$ and thereby determine both band energies and eigenvectors used subsequently in response calculations.

Note the self-consistency tension between chosen TB overlap/transfer parameters and realistic atomic orbitals. The overlap parameters (for example $s$) are by definition the integrals of products of atomic orbitals on neighbouring sites, $s=\langle\varphi_A|\varphi_B\rangle$, so for a given choice of microscopic atomic wavefunctions $\varphi_j(\mathbf{x})$ one can compute $s$ directly. Conversely, TB practitioners often fix $s$ and $t$ to reproduce measured band dispersions; this implies constraints on the shapes of the underlying atomic orbitals. The TB approximation does not provide a microscopic mechanism to produce atomic orbitals that simultaneously (i) match realistic isolated-atom wavefunctions (e.g. Roothaan–Hartree–Fock (RHF) orbitals) and (ii) yield the overlap parameters required by the empirical TB parametrisation.

Describe attempts to reconcile TB overlap parameters with atomic orbitals and the demonstrated incompatibility. One procedure is to adopt hydrogenic orbitals with rescaled effective charges $Z_{\text{eff}}$ and tune $Z_{\text{eff}}$ so that the computed overlaps match the TB parameters; this reproduces the overlap integrals but yields atomic orbitals that markedly deviate from RHF atomic wavefunctions (compare radial and momentum-space profiles). Conversely, using genuine RHF atomic orbitals produces overlap integrals that do not equal the TB $s$ and $t$ parameters; rescaling RHF orbitals to force agreement spoils their fidelity to carbon atomic physics. This incompatibility is quantified by comparing the radial and momentum-space forms of hydrogenic, rescaled, and RHF orbitals (see the wavefunction comparisons), which shows large deviations when imposing TB overlap consistency. Fig.11

Explain the practical consequence for high-momentum components of the material response $W(\boldsymbol{\ell},E_e)$. Electron momentum-density contributions at large initial-state momentum $|\boldsymbol{\ell}|$ are governed by the behavior of the atomic-like orbitals close to the nuclei. Since the TB embedding ambiguity alters orbital shapes in the atomic-core region when overlap parameters are enforced, TB predictions for the high-$\ell$ tail of $W$ are intrinsically uncertain. This is corroborated by the head-to-head comparison with DFT, which shows TB predicting significantly larger $W(\ell)$ than DFT for $\ell\gtrsim 15\ \mathrm{keV}$, indicating that the TB embedding ambiguity plausibly causes TB to overestimate high-momentum contributions. Fig.4

Conclude that this unresolved embedding ambiguity is an intrinsic limitation of standard TB implementations for applications requiring accurate high-momentum initial-state electron densities. The TB approximation lacks a self-consistent mechanism to produce atomic orbitals that both reproduce the empirically chosen overlap/transfer parameters and maintain fidelity to realistic atomic wavefunctions; therefore, TB-based predictions of $W$ at large $\ell$ (and hence rate predictions for interactions that weight large momentum transfer) remain uncertain unless either (i) a principled renormalization of atomic orbitals within TB is developed that preserves atomic fidelity, or (ii) first-principles methods (such as DFT) are preferred for the material input.

motivating_questions.content: The TB approximation is phenomenological: it assumes the existence of localized atomic-like orbitals whose overlap and transfer integrals reproduce the material band structure, but it does not provide a unique microscopic construction of those orbitals. For applications (like DM-induced electron ejection) that are sensitive to the detailed high-momentum tail of initial-state wavefunctions, this ambiguity matters because the TB overlap parameters imply constraints on orbital shapes that realistic atomic orbitals (RHF) do not satisfy. Without a self-consistent embedding strategy, TB-based predictions of $W$ at large $\ell$ remain uncertain; resolving this would require either a principled renormalization of atomic orbitals within TB that preserves atomic fidelity or preference for first-principles DFT-derived momentum densities.

The workflow is reported to increase SL bandgap prediction accuracy, at the expense of increased computational cost in the genetic-algorithm optimization.

steps.reasoning: Define the computational fitting objective: the empirical tight-binding method (ETBM) bulk Hamiltonian in the $sp^{3}s^{*}$, first-nearest-neighbor, spin–orbit-including approximation contains 15 orbital-interaction parameters (these are scalar energy parameters that enter the bulk Hamiltonian matrix). The fitting goal is to determine a reduced set of free parameters whose optimized values reproduce selected bulk experimental band energies and effective masses and also yield accurate superlattice (SL) predictions when SL Hamiltonians are constructed from the bulk parameters.

Define the fitting reduction strategy used to reduce the number of free parameters from 15 to 9: treat the two atomic spin–orbit constants $\Delta_{a}$ and $\Delta_{c}$ (where $\Delta_{a}$ is the anion atomic spin–orbit coupling energy and $\Delta_{c}$ is the cation atomic spin–orbit coupling energy) as fixed atomic constants taken from prior semi-empirical tabulations, and enforce four analytic relations that arise from the $\Gamma$-point symmetry analysis (these four relations provide algebraic constraints among some orbital-energy parameters at the $\Gamma$ point). This choice reduces the number of independent fitted orbital-interaction parameters to nine.
[12]

Define the optimization algorithm and cost-function augmentation: use a genetic algorithm (GA) (where GA denotes genetic algorithm) to optimize the nine free orbital-interaction parameters by minimizing a scalar cost function that sums absolute differences between calculated and experimental target values. The cost function includes bulk targets (band energies and effective masses at multiple high-symmetry points in the first Brillouin zone) and, critically, includes at least one experimental SL bandgap target (an experimental superlattice gap value) as an explicit entry in the cost-function target list; inclusion of an SL experimental gap in the GA cost increases computational cost and complicates the cost landscape but is reported to improve SL prediction accuracy.

Specify the data used in the GA: the authors fitted to 27 bulk experimental data points (band energies and effective masses at various symmetry points) drawn from the literature at 300 K and augmented the GA target set with one experimental SL bandgap value (yielding 28 targets total for fitting), so that the GA optimizes the nine free orbital-interaction parameters to simultaneously reproduce bulk and at least one SL datum.

Describe how SL Hamiltonians are constructed from the bulk parameters once the bulk parameters are obtained: (a) include strain effects by deforming the spatial (Bloch-phase) part of orbital-interaction matrix elements according to lattice-mismatch-induced deformation of bond vectors (the spatial part of orbital overlap is modified to account for stress/strain), (b) include energy band-lineup (band-offset) effects by adding band-lineup offsets to diagonal Hamiltonian elements using the model-solid prescription for band lineups (where the model-solid prescription denotes the Van de Walle model-solid theory for band lineups), and (c) treat interface atomic parameters by averaging the bulk atomic orbital-interaction parameters for atoms at hetero-interfaces (interface-atom averaging) to produce mixed-interface Hamiltonian matrix elements. These prescriptions define how a SL Hamiltonian matrix is assembled from the bulk parameter set for a specified sequence of monolayers.
[22]

State the practical trade-offs that follow from this workflow: including an experimental SL gap in the GA cost helps the fitted bulk parameters transfer to accurate SL predictions, but it increases GA computational expense and complicates the cost landscape (raising potential overfitting concerns); similarly, the chosen prescriptions for strain deformation of Bloch-phase spatial factors, band-lineup offsets, and interface-atom averaging are modeling choices that materially affect SL results and therefore must be documented to ensure reproducibility and to explain improved SL accuracy.

motivating_questions.content: Conventional ETB parameter fitting typically targets only bulk band-structure data and may therefore fail to reproduce superlattice bandgaps without manual adjustment. Incorporating explicit SL experimental targets into the fitting objective promises better SL predictions but raises practical issues: the cost function becomes more complex and computational expense grows, and model choices (how to treat interface atoms, strain-induced modification of spatial orbital overlaps, and band-lineup prescriptions) substantially affect SL Hamiltonian construction. A documented workflow that (a) includes an SL experimental target in GA fitting and (b) prescribes strain, band-lineup and interface-averaging rules is therefore needed so that fitted parameters transfer to SL predictions in a reproducible way.

steps.reasoning: Define the electronic-structure model and notation: $sp^3d^5s^*$ denotes a nearest-neighbor tight-binding Hamiltonian basis composed of atomic orbitals $s$, $p_x,p_y,p_z$, five $d$ orbitals, and an excited $s^*$ orbital for each atom; "TB" abbreviates tight-binding; "optical critical-point transition energies" denote the energies of strong interband optical transitions commonly labeled $E_1$, $E_1+\Delta_1$, $E_0^{\prime}$, and $E_2$, where $\Delta_1$ and $\Delta_0$ denote spin-orbit splittings at the corresponding critical points.

State the fitting objectives and rationale: for atomistic fullband optical-response calculations one requires a Hamiltonian that reproduces not only band-edge energies and effective masses but also optical critical-point energies and transition matrix elements across the Brillouin zone; therefore the parameter set to be determined must have targets that include the conduction-band minima energies at the symmetry points $\Gamma$, $L$, and $X$ (each energy measured with respect to the valence-band maximum), the valence-band split-off energies, effective masses at these points, and the optical critical-point energies $E_1$, $E_1+\Delta_1$, $E_0^{\prime}$, and $E_2$.

Formulate the optimization problem: the nearest-neighbor $sp^3d^5s^*$ model contains 31 independent parameters (8 on-site energies, 21 two-center hopping integrals, and 2 spin-orbit interaction energies); fitting these 31 parameters is a 31-dimensional nonlinear global optimization problem whose objective is to minimize weighted deviations between TB-generated band parameters and the target room-temperature experimental/reference values for the energies and effective masses specified above.

Describe the optimization algorithm and computational workflow used to obtain the parameters: initialize the 31 TB parameters randomly within reasonable parameter bounds to form chromosomes; use a parallel genetic algorithm (PGAPack) to evolve a population of chromosomes through selection, crossover, and mutation; for each chromosome evaluate the $sp^3d^5s^*$ TB solver to compute the band energies, effective masses, and optical transition energies and compute a weighted fitness score comparing those outputs to the specified room-temperature target values; iterate generations until convergence criteria (stability of generations or identical chromosomes) are met, yielding an optimized parameter set. 
PGAPack⁵³

Account for room-temperature effects in the fitting and validation: apply hydrostatic tensile strain to low-temperature parametrizations where necessary to represent room-temperature lattice expansion (i.e., adjust lattice constant from $a(0\mathrm{K})$ to $a(300\mathrm{K})$ when comparing to low-temperature parameter sets), and when comparing to quasiparticle calculations performed at low temperature, shift conduction bands by an empirically chosen offset (for example, the quasiparticle self-consistent GW conduction bands were shifted by $-0.1\ \mathrm{eV}$ to approximate temperature effects) and shift valence bands appropriately to compare band-shape features.

Present the optimized parameter outcome and immediate electronic-structure outputs: the optimized nearest-neighbor $sp^3d^5s^*$ parameters (tabulated in the work) produce fullband electronic dispersions along high-symmetry lines for GaAs and GaP at room temperature with the valence-band maxima aligned to 0 eV; these dispersions were plotted and directly compared to a quasiparticle self-consistent GW (QSGW) calculation (with the QSGW conduction bands shifted by $-0.1\ \mathrm{eV}$ and the QSGW second-top valence band shifted by $-0.34\ \mathrm{eV}$ to enable shape comparison), showing general agreement in conduction- and valence-band shapes, particularly for the lowest conduction band between $L$ and $\Gamma$ and for the split-off valence band.

Conclude the practical adequacy of the optimized parameter sets for optical-response modeling: because the optimization explicitly targeted room-temperature conduction-band energies at $\Gamma$, $L$, and $X$, valence-band split-off energies, effective masses, and optical critical-point energies $E_1$, $E_1+\Delta_1$, $E_0^{\prime}$, and $E_2$, and because the resulting fullband electronic structures and computed $\varepsilon_2(\omega)$ and absorption coefficients reproduce the main experimental critical-point positions and spectral features at room temperature for both GaP and GaAs while producing conduction-band energies and effective masses comparable to reference compilations, the optimized nearest-neighbor $sp^3d^5s^*$ tight-binding parameter sets for GaP and GaAs are established as suitable for subsequent fullband optical-response calculations.

motivating_questions.content: For atomistic fullband optical-response calculations one needs a Hamiltonian that yields not only accurate band edges and effective masses, but also optical critical-point energies and transition matrix elements over the entire Brillouin zone. Existing $sp^3d^5s^*$ parameter sets in the literature were often fitted to low-temperature band edges or to subsets of band parameters and therefore did not guarantee accurate optical spectra at room temperature: optical critical points ($E_1$, $E_2$, $E_0'$, etc.) could be misplaced or peak shapes mismatched. First-principles quasiparticle methods can produce accurate dispersions but are computationally expensive to tune across compositions and can systematically over- or under-estimate some gaps; hence an empirical, fullband tight-binding parameter set explicitly fitted to optical transition energies was needed to enable efficient, composition-resolved calculations of dielectric functions and absorption for dilute-N alloys.

reasoning_chains.conclusion_text: A compact, transferable nonorthogonal spd tight-binding parametrization for first-row transition metals (Cr, Fe, Co) was developed. Hopping and overlap matrix elements take exponential distance dependence (Hamiltonian integrals $\sim f_0 e^{-q d}$, overlaps $\sim s_0 e^{-q d}$) with specified canonical ratios and modified nonorthogonal ratios ($dd\sigma:dd\pi:dd\delta=-6f_0:5f_0:-2.2f_0$, $pp\sigma:pp\pi=2:-1$), fixed on-site $s$ and $p$ energies (0.2 Ry and 0.45 Ry relative to $d$), and Stoner $I$ values adjusted to reproduce LSDA moments. The parameter set is listed in Table I of the paper and is sufficient, without system-specific refitting, to produce densities of states and magnetic moments in good quantitative agreement with full LSDA calculations for bcc-Fe ($m\approx2.18\mu_B$), antiferromagnetic Cr ($m\approx0.74\mu_B$), and Co phases, and to reproduce key energetic trends (see comparisons below).

The tight-binding total energy including magnetic terms may be written as $E_{\mathrm{tot}}=E_{1}+E_{2}$ with
      $$
      E_{1}=\sum_{\sigma}\operatorname{Tr}\bigl[\hat{\rho}^{\sigma} H_{0}\bigr]+E_{\mathrm{pair}}
      $$
      and
      $$
      E_{2}=\tfrac{1}{2}\sum_{\mathbf{R}}\Bigl\{\sum_{L}Q_{\mathbf{R}L}V_{\mathbf{R}L}^{M}+\bigl(U_{\mathbf{R}}-\tfrac{1}{2}I_{\mathbf{R}}\bigr)\delta q_{\mathbf{R}}^{2}-\tfrac{1}{2}I_{\mathbf{R}}m_{\mathbf{R}}^{2}\Bigr\},
      $$
      where $H_{0}$ is the non-self-consistent tight-binding Hamiltonian generated from the non-spin-polarized reference density $\rho_{\mathrm{in}}$, $\hat{\rho}^{\sigma}$ is the spin density matrix, $E_{\mathrm{pair}}$ is the short-range repulsive pair energy representing the Harris–Foulkes remainder, $\mathbf{R}$ labels atomic sites, $Q_{\mathbf{R}L}$ are self-consistent multipole moments at site $\mathbf{R}$ with composite index $L=\{\ell m\}$, $V_{\mathbf{R}L}^{M}$ are the corresponding Madelung potentials, $\delta q_{\mathbf{R}}$ is the site monopole (charge) change, and $m_{\mathbf{R}}$ is the local moment. The magnetic contribution enters as an explicit $-\tfrac{1}{2}I_{\mathbf{R}}m_{\mathbf{R}}^{2}$ term per site.

steps.reasoning:
State the aim and minimal functional forms chosen for the tight-binding parametrization: adopt a nonorthogonal $spd$ basis including $s$, $p$, and $d$ orbitals per atom, use exponentially decaying distance dependence for Hamiltonian two-center integrals and overlaps, and employ a simple pair potential of exponential form for short-range repulsion. Specifically, Hamiltonian integrals are taken proportional to $f_0 e^{-q d}$ and overlap matrix elements proportional to $s_0 e^{-q d}$, where $d$ is the interatomic distance, $f_0$ and $s_0$ are prefactors, and $q$ is an exponent. This choice follows the Spanjaard and Desjonquères spirit but extended in range and basis. 
[48]

Specify the canonical and modified nonorthogonal orbital ratio rules and on-site level offsets: for $dd$ Hamiltonian integrals adopt the nonorthogonal modified canonical ratios
$
dd\sigma:dd\pi:dd\delta=-6f_0:5f_0:-2.2f_0,
$
and for $pp$ integrals use
$
pp\sigma:pp\pi=2:-1.
$
Fix the on-site $s$ and $p$ atomic level energies relative to the $d$ level at $0.2\ \mathrm{Ry}$ and $0.45\ \mathrm{Ry}$ respectively. These choices reduce the number of free parameters and impose transferability.

Specify the range, exponents, and numerical choices used for the distance dependence and band filling: use the same exponent $q$ for Hamiltonian and overlap matrix elements (but different prefactors $f_0$ and $s_0$), set $q d_0^{\mathrm{bcc}}=3$ for all $dd$ interactions where $d_0$ is equilibrium bond length in bcc, otherwise use $q=0.5\ \mathrm{bohr}^{-1}$, and set the number of $d$ electrons in the $d$-only model where used to $N_d=6$ when needed to place the Fermi level appropriately in the density of states comparisons. These numeric choices are part of the compact parametrization.

List the parameters are collated into a single tabulation and adjust $f_0$ and $I$ to reproduce LDA bandwidths and moments: assemble the full parameter set (Hamiltonian prefactors $f_0$, overlap prefactors $s_0$, on-site $s$ and $p$ energies, pair-potential parameter $B$, and Stoner $I$ per element) into a table (Table I) and adjust $f_0$ to reproduce the $d$-bandwidth from LSDA calculations and adjust the Stoner parameter $I$ to reproduce LSDA magnetic moments. The resulting compact parameter set is presented in Table I of the paper. 
Table I

Demonstrate transferability and validation by comparing calculated densities of states and moments for key elements: using the parameter set without system-specific refitting, produce self-consistent tight-binding densities of states and magnetic moments for bcc-Fe, antiferromagnetic Cr, and Co phases and compare quantitatively to LSDA. For bcc-Fe the self-consistent tight-binding predicts a moment $m\approx2.18\mu_B$ in close agreement with LSDA; for antiferromagnetic Cr the tight-binding local moment $m\approx0.74\mu_B$ matches the LSDA estimate $0.70\mu_B$; Co phases are also described with reasonable transferability. These comparisons and the claim that the parametrization is sufficient without system-specific refitting are supported by plotted DOS comparisons and tabulated energetic data presented in the paper (e.g., Fig. 3 and Fig. 4 and the tabulated results).

Fig. 4

motivating_questions.content: Predictive tight-binding requires a parameter set that is as simple as possible yet transferable across crystal structures and compositions so that one may compute electronic structure and energetics without refitting for each application. Prior orthogonal $d$-only or non-self-consistent models either missed crucial $sd$ hybridization effects or required ad hoc adjustments to place the Fermi level at desired features. There was a need for (i) an spd nonorthogonal parametrization that reproduces the fine structure of the density of states near the Fermi level, (ii) transferability among bcc/hcp/fcc environments, and (iii) parameter economy so that band widths and volumes can be adjusted with minimal free parameters while retaining fidelity to LSDA electronic structure and magnetic moments.

steps.reasoning: Construct the tight-binding (TB) part of the total Hamiltonian by defining $H_{0}$ as the lattice sum of transfer energies between molecular orbitals: $H_{0}=\sum_{i,j=1}^{N}\sum_{\alpha,\beta=1}^{4}\sum_{s,s'=\pm}t_{i,j;\alpha s,\beta s'}a_{i,\alpha,s}^{\dagger}a_{j,\beta,s'}$, where $a_{i,\alpha,s}^{\dagger}$ ($a_{j,\beta,s'}$) creates (annihilates) an electron on molecule $\alpha$ ($\beta$) in unit cell $i$ ($j$) with spin $s$ ($s'$), $N$ is the number of unit cells, and $t_{i,j;\alpha s,\beta s'}$ denotes the transfer energy between the two MLWF-centered orbitals; the transfer energy is defined from maximally localized Wannier functions (MLWFs) by $t_{\alpha,\beta;\sigma,\sigma'}(\mathbf{R})=\langle\phi_{\alpha,\sigma,0}|H|\phi_{\beta,\sigma',\mathbf{R}}\rangle$, where $\phi_{\alpha,\sigma,\mathbf{R}}$ denotes the MLWF localized on molecule $\alpha$ with spin $\sigma$ and centered at lattice vector $\mathbf{R}$, and $\sigma=\pm$ denotes spin up/down.

Obtain first-principles electronic structure including spin-orbit coupling (SOC) by performing full-relativistic density functional theory (DFT) calculations with plane-wave basis sets and norm-conserving pseudopotentials; then select the set of low-energy bands to be represented by MLWFs and construct MLWFs using the wannier90 code to represent the molecular HOMO-derived bands near the Fermi level, thereby enabling computation of the MLWF overlaps that give the TB transfer energies $t_{i,j;\alpha s,\beta s'}$ as matrix elements of the ab initio Hamiltonian. 
[42]
[43]

From the MLWF overlaps computed in the previous step, extract the TB transfer energies for nearest-neighbor (NN) and next-nearest-neighbor (NNN) bonds and for same-spin and opposite-spin channels; denote a generic same-spin transfer by $w_{h,s=s'}$ and an opposite-spin (spin-flip) transfer by $w_{h,s=-s'}$; observe that inclusion of SOC in the DFT produces complex-valued transfer energies, i.e., each transfer acquires a real part $\mathrm{Re}(w_h)$ and an imaginary part $\mathrm{Im}(w_h)$, so the model contains both real and imaginary transfer-energy contributions originating from SOC.
Table I

Introduce site-potential differences to capture Hartree and chemical-environment contributions that improve the fit to the low-energy ab initio bands: define $\Delta V_{B}=V_{B}-V_{A}$ and $\Delta V_{C}=V_{C}-V_{A}$, where $V_{\alpha}=\langle\phi_{\alpha,\sigma,0}|H|\phi_{\alpha,\sigma',0}\rangle$ is the MLWF on-site energy for molecule $\alpha$; determine the numerical values $\Delta V_{B}=-0.0047\ \mathrm{eV}$ and $\Delta V_{C}=-0.0092\ \mathrm{eV}$ from the MLWF matrix elements reported in the TB parameter set.
Table I

Assemble the four-band TB Hamiltonian $H_{0}+H_{1}$ (where $H_{1}=\Delta V_{B}\hat{n}_{B}+\Delta V_{C}\hat{n}_{C}$ with $\hat{n}_{\alpha}=\sum_{\boldsymbol{k},s}a_{\alpha s}^{\dagger}(\boldsymbol{k})a_{\alpha s}(\boldsymbol{k})$) into the momentum-space matrix $h_{\alpha s,\beta s'}(\boldsymbol{k})$ and diagonalize it to obtain band eigenvalues $E_{\gamma}(\boldsymbol{k})$ ($\gamma=1,\dots,4$) and eigenvectors $d_{\alpha s\gamma}(\boldsymbol{k})$; use these eigenvalues to compare directly with the first-principles DFT band energies at high-symmetry (time-reversal invariant) momenta.

Validate the TB model by comparing the TB band energies computed from the MLWF-derived parameters (including both real and imaginary parts of the transfers and the site-potential shifts $\Delta V_{B}$ and $\Delta V_{C}$) with the full-relativistic DFT band structure: the TB eigenvalues at the time-reversal invariant momenta agree with the DFT band energies within approximately $0.01\ \mathrm{eV}$, demonstrating that the four-band TB Hamiltonian reproduces the ab initio band energies at TRIM to the stated accuracy.

motivating_questions.content: To theoretically scrutinize the electronic properties of α-(BETS)₂I₃—a molecular Dirac system with strong SOC—a low-energy Hamiltonian that faithfully reflects the full ab initio band structure is indispensable. Earlier attempts to extract tight-binding parameters for this material faced the challenge that many transfer integrals contribute in a narrow energy window around the Dirac points, and efficient methods for incorporating SOC into effective models had not been established for such complex molecular solids. Without a reliable tight-binding model, the calculation of transport coefficients, the role of the imaginary transfer energies, and quantitative comparisons with experiment remained out of reach.

steps.reasoning: Explain the operational problem motivating targeted validation: tight-binding models are often developed to enable calculations for large or complex systems that are not tractable with fully ab initio DFT, so users routinely build TB parameterizations on small unit cells and then deploy them to larger-scale simulations; therefore, ensuring that a chosen TB parameterization predicts the specific observable of interest prior to large-scale deployment is important to guard against misleading results.

Record the authors' methodological recommendation and supporting rationale: the authors explicitly state that "models should be tested on the property of interest" and emphasize that such validations "can be performed on small unit cells before scaling the model to larger systems or systems that include additional interactions" and that performing these targeted validations "does not mitigate the advantages of using a tight-binding model" because the computational savings of TB remain available for large-scale applications once the model is validated on the small reference cell.

Summarize the procedural prescription derived from the paper's results: before deploying a TB model to large or complex systems, validate the model against first-principles calculations of the specific optical observable (for example, compute $\mathrm{Im}[\varepsilon_{xx}(\omega)]$ and $\sigma_{yyY}(\omega)$ from both DFT restricted to the same bands and from the TB model on the small unit cell and compare); such targeted validation will reveal deficiencies (for example, wavefunction-dependent matrix-element errors) that are not apparent from band-energy RMSE alone and ensures model reliability for the intended application without eliminating the computational advantages of TB for larger systems.

motivating_questions.content: A common workflow is to fit TB parameters on small cells and then scale the model to large systems without property-specific validation, under the implicit assumption that band-energy agreement suffices. If band agreement alone is insufficient for optical properties, as established for MoS2, then models can produce erroneous predictions at large scale. The practical resolution is to require small-cell, property-specific benchmarking against DFT for the observable of interest; doing so identifies deficiencies (in orbital basis, hopping range, or wavefunction fidelity) before large-scale calculations are attempted, thereby preserving TB efficiency while ensuring predictive accuracy.

premises.content:
A semi-empirical tight-binding parametrization was established for CdS, CdTe, ZnS and ZnTe using a second-nearest-neighbor ($2\ \text{nn}$) $sp^{3}s^{*}$ basis including spin–orbit coupling. The electronic eigenvalue problem solved is the usual tight-binding secular equation
      $$
      \sum_{\beta}\left[H_{\alpha\beta}(k)-S_{\alpha\beta}(k)E\right]u_{\beta}=0,
      $$

premises.content:
A $20\times20$ nearest-neighbor tight-binding Hamiltonian for the two-atom zincblende basis using the $sp^3d^5s^*$ orbital set (10 orbitals per atom: $s$, $p_x$, $p_y$, $p_z$, $d_{xz}$, $d_{yz}$, $d_{xy}$, $d_{x^2-y^2}$, $d_{3r^2-z^2}$, $s^*$) is constructed by placing the Slater–Koster-derived matrix elements, obtained from the two-center integral relations and structure factors, into a matrix with rows and columns ordered by the orbital sequence on the cation and then the anion. Spin–orbit coupling is included by duplicating the $20\times20$ block for spin-up and spin-down to form a block-diagonal matrix and then adding a spin–orbit coupling correction matrix $H^\Delta$, so that the full Hamiltonian is
      $$
      H = \begin{bmatrix} H_{sp^3d^5s^*} & 0\\[4pt] 0 & H_{sp^3d^5s^*} \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} H_{11}^{\Delta} & H_{12}^{\Delta}\\[4pt] H_{21}^{\Delta} & H_{22}^{\Delta} \end{bmatrix},
      $$
      producing an explicit $40\times40$ Hamiltonian. The spin–orbit correction is implemented only on the $p$-orbital subspace (neglecting the much smaller contribution from excited $d$ states) using two coupling parameters $\delta_a$ and $\delta_c$ (with $\delta_{a,c}=\Delta_{a,c}/3$). The sparse block matrices $H_{ij}^\Delta$ have nonzero entries only in the $p$-orbital subspace: $H_{11}^\Delta$ has $i\delta_a$ on the cation $p_x$ diagonal and $-i\delta_a$ on the cation $p_y$ diagonal, and similarly $i\delta_c$ and $-i\delta_c$ on the corresponding anion orbitals; $H_{22}^\Delta$ has $-i\delta_a$ and $i\delta_a$ on the same diagonal positions; $H_{12}^\Delta$ and $H_{21}^\Delta$ contain off-diagonal entries coupling the $p$ orbitals between the two spin blocks, as defined by the spin–orbit coupling formalism.

The cost function and constrained Nelder–Mead procedure described above address these methodological needs, producing parameter sets that reproduce both energies and effective masses in a physically consistent manner.

With appropriately chosen $(t_0,t_1,t_2)$ the tight-binding band structures qualitatively reproduce the band dispersions of the optimized photonic crystal (PtC) and the parity distributions at the high-symmetry points $\Gamma$ and $X$: the TE-mode parity distribution is closely matched; the TM-mode parity distribution is qualitatively consistent in its topological invariants (odd or even count of opposite-sign parity pairs) though the specific parity at each band is not reproduced because the three short-range hopping terms cannot capture the full parity distribution of the continuum PtC. These lattice models exhibit an odd number of bands per unit cell and show that the entire band manifold can be topological for one choice of unit cell — a behavior that differs from the standard two-dimensional square Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSH) model which has an even number of bands and whose full band manifold is topologically trivial for both unit-cell choices.

conclusion.content:
A neural-network tight-binding Hamiltonian construction (TBHCNN) parametrizes the elements of a real-space tight-binding (TB) Hamiltonian matrix H by assigning one trainable real-valued neuron to each matrix element (on-site energies $\epsilon_i$ on the diagonal and hopping terms $t_{ij}$ off-diagonal), so that the reciprocal-space TB Hamiltonian for wavevector $\mathbf{k}$ is $H^{\mathrm{TB}}(\mathbf{k})=\sum_{\mathbf{R}} e^{i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{R}}H^{0\mathbf{R}}$, where the set $\{H^{0\mathbf{R}}\}$ are the selected real-space Hamiltonian matrices labeled by lattice vectors $\mathbf{R}$. The network is trained using only the ab-initio reference energy eigenvalues $\varepsilon_{i,\mathbf{k}}^{\mathrm{Ab}}$ for a chosen set of $N$ bands indexed by $i=1,\dots,N$ and a chosen set of $N_{\mathbf{k}}$ sampled $\mathbf{k}$-points, by minimizing the mean squared error loss
      $$
      \Delta_E=\mathrm{Loss}=\frac{1}{N}\frac{1}{N_{\mathbf{k}}}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\sum_{\mathbf{k}}\left(\varepsilon_{i,\mathbf{k}}^{\mathrm{TB}}-\varepsilon_{i,\mathbf{k}}^{\mathrm{Ab}}\right)^2,
      $$
      where $\varepsilon_{i,\mathbf{k}}^{\mathrm{TB}}$ are the eigenvalues of $H^{\mathrm{TB}}(\mathbf{k})$ and all symbols ($N$, $N_{\mathbf{k}}$, indices $i$, $\mathbf{k}$) are as defined above. Gradients of the loss with respect to the real-space Hamiltonian elements are computed by algorithmic differentiation and combined across $\mathbf{k}$ as
      $$
      \overline{H^{0\mathbf{R}}}=\sum_{\mathbf{k}} e^{i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{R}}\,\Psi_{\mathbf{k}}\;\overline{E}_{\mathbf{k}}\;\Psi_{\mathbf{k}}^{T},
      $$
      with $\Psi_{\mathbf{k}}=(\psi_{1,\mathbf{k}}^{\mathrm{TB}},\psi_{2,\mathbf{k}}^{\mathrm{TB}},\dots,\psi_{N,\mathbf{k}}^{\mathrm{TB}})$ the matrix whose columns are the TB eigenvectors $\psi_{n,\mathbf{k}}^{\mathrm{TB}}$, and $\overline{E}_{\mathbf{k}}=\mathrm{diag}\!\left(\partial\mathrm{Loss}/\partial\varepsilon_{1,\mathbf{k}}^{\mathrm{TB}},\dots,\partial\mathrm{Loss}/\partial\varepsilon_{N,\mathbf{k}}^{\mathrm{TB}}\right)$ the diagonal matrix of loss derivatives with respect to the TB eigenvalues; these gradient tensors are then used in a gradient-descent update $H_{n+1}^{0\mathbf{R}}=H_{n}^{0\mathbf{R}}-\alpha\,\overline{H_{n}^{0\mathbf{R}}}$ with learning rate $\alpha$ to change the neuron values. No orbital labels, atomic coordinates, or ab-initio eigenfunction information are required as inputs to this training protocol. If the loss remains above a predefined threshold after a user-specified maximum number of training steps, the TBHCNN increases the number of neurons (thereby enlarging the TB basis by a preset increment), reinitializes the added neurons (initial values drawn from a standard normal distribution), and continues training; this procedure provides an automated, iterative determination of the basis size for the selected set of reference bands.

steps.reasoning: The starting point is the stated need for a fast tight-binding (TB) parameterization method that can reproduce ab-initio band energies without requiring basis-function information, atomic-coordinate information, or a manual fitting procedure. The paper contrasts this need with empirical TB models, which are not transferable across geometries, and projection-based ab-initio TB methods, which require eigenfunctions, basis selection, and may suffer truncation error. [4-10, 16-22, 23-24]

The method introduces a neural network (NN) in which the neurons themselves are the TB matrix elements, so the trainable variables are the on-site energies $\epsilon_i$ and hopping terms $t_{ij}$ that form the real-space Hamiltonian matrix. The parametrized TB Hamiltonian is written as $H = \sum_i \epsilon_i n_i + \sum_{i \neq j} t_{ij} c_i^\dagger c_j$, where $n_i$ is the number operator at site $i$, $c_i^\dagger$ is the creation operator, and $c_j$ is the annihilation operator. This means the NN is not used as a generic input-output predictor, but as a direct parameterization of the Hamiltonian itself. [4, 23, 24]

The only training data are selected ab-initio band energies $\varepsilon^{\mathrm{Ab}}_{i,\mathbf{k}}$, where $i$ indexes the reference bands and $\mathbf{k}$ is the crystal momentum. The mismatch between the TB and ab-initio energies is measured by the mean squared error
        $$
        \Delta_E = \frac{1}{N}\frac{1}{N_{\mathbf{k}}}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\sum_{\mathbf{k}}\left(\varepsilon^{\mathrm{TB}}_{i,\mathbf{k}}-\varepsilon^{\mathrm{Ab}}_{i,\mathbf{k}}\right)^2,
        $$
        and this quantity is used as the loss function. Here $N$ is the number of selected bands and $N_{\mathbf{k}}$ is the number of sampled $\mathbf{k}$ points. [23, 24, 27]

The forward pass constructs the reciprocal-space TB Hamiltonian from the real-space Hamiltonian matrices $H^{0\mathbf{R}}$ by
        $$
        H^{\mathrm{TB}}(\mathbf{k}) = \sum_{\mathbf{R}} e^{i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{R}} H^{0\mathbf{R}},
        $$
        and diagonalizes it through
        $$
        H^{\mathrm{TB}}(\mathbf{k})\psi_{n,\mathbf{k}}^{\mathrm{TB}} = \varepsilon_{n,\mathbf{k}}^{\mathrm{TB}}\psi_{n,\mathbf{k}}^{\mathrm{TB}}.
        $$
        The backward pass then uses algorithmic differentiation to compute the derivative of the loss with respect to each real-space Hamiltonian matrix element:
        $$
        \overline{H^{0\mathbf{R}}} = \sum_{\mathbf{k}} e^{i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{R}}\Psi_{\mathbf{k}}\overline{E}_{\mathbf{k}}\Psi_{\mathbf{k}}^{T},
        $$
        where $\Psi_{\mathbf{k}} = (\psi_{1,\mathbf{k}}^{\mathrm{TB}}, \psi_{2,\mathbf{k}}^{\mathrm{TB}}, \dots, \psi_{n,\mathbf{k}}^{\mathrm{TB}})$ and
        $$
        \overline{E}_{\mathbf{k}} = \mathrm{diag}\!\left(\frac{\partial \mathrm{Loss}}{\partial \varepsilon_{1,\mathbf{k}}^{\mathrm{TB}}}, \frac{\partial \mathrm{Loss}}{\partial \varepsilon_{2,\mathbf{k}}^{\mathrm{TB}}}, \dots, \frac{\partial \mathrm{Loss}}{\partial \varepsilon_{N,\mathbf{k}}^{\mathrm{TB}}}\right).
        $$
        The Hamiltonian parameters are updated by gradient descent,
        $$
        H_{n+1}^{0\mathbf{R}} = H_n^{0\mathbf{R}} - \alpha \overline{H_n^{0\mathbf{R}}},
        $$
        where $\alpha$ is the learning rate and $n$ counts the training step. [27, 23, 24, 51]

Training proceeds until the loss reaches a predefined threshold. If the threshold is not reached after a maximum number of steps, extra neurons are added to enlarge the real-space Hamiltonian basis, the network is reinitialized, and a new training round begins. The paper states that this dynamic enlargement continues until a satisfactory match is obtained, and that no manual intervention is needed. [23, 24]

Because the training uses only ab-initio band energies and does not require basis functions, atomic coordinates, or eigenfunctions, and because the Hamiltonian parameters are adjusted directly by back-propagation with automatic basis-size enlargement when needed, the method is established as a neural-network TB Hamiltonian parameterization scheme that works without basis functions and with automated basis-size determination. The paper names this approach TBHCNN. [23, 24]

motivating_questions.content: In the context of transport‑property simulations, a fast and reliable tight‑binding (TB) model is needed that can reproduce the ab‑initio band structure of a specific material without the intervention of an expert. Empirical TB models built from previously published parameter sets are not transferable across different geometries and lose quantitative accuracy. Projection‑based ab‑initio TB methods, while more accurate, demand full knowledge of ab‑initio wavefunctions and the manual selection or iterative optimization of basis functions, which is time‑consuming and requires detailed physical insight. Moreover, when the desired TB representation restricts the interaction range (e.g., to nearest neighbours), the necessary truncation of long‑range hopping elements introduces an inherent accuracy loss. Therefore, a method was lacking that could construct a system‑specific TB Hamiltonian automatically, using only the ab‑initio band energies as input, without any basis‑function knowledge, and that would completely avoid truncation error.

premises.content: For the 6.4 nm GaBiAs quantum wells with nominal Bi composition 2.2% (samples 3, 5, and 6), the constrained 12-band $k \cdot p$ model overestimates the splitting between the first heavy-hole state (hh1) and the first light-hole state (lh1) (hh1-lh1 splitting) by 10-13 meV. For sample 3 (a 6.4 nm GaBi$_{0.022}$As$_{0.978}$/Al$_{0.074}$Ga$_{0.926}$As single quantum well), the calculated splitting is 37.1 meV while the measured splitting is 27 meV (an overestimate of 10.1 meV). For sample 5 (a 6.4 nm GaBi$_{0.022}$As$_{0.978}$/Al$_{0.144}$Ga$_{0.856}$As single quantum well), the calculated transition from the first confined electron state (e1) to lh1 is at 1.311 eV while the measured value is 1.301 eV, and the e1 to hh1 transition is reproduced within 1 meV (1.273 vs 1.274 eV), implying a calculated splitting of approximately 38 meV compared to a measured splitting of approximately 27 meV (overestimate of ~11 meV). For sample 6 (6.4 nm GaBi$_{0.022}$As$_{0.978}$/GaAs single quantum well), the calculated e1-lh1 transition is at 1.273 eV while the measured value is 1.264 eV, a 9 meV discrepancy, with the e1-hh1 reproduced within 1 meV, implying an overestimate of ~9 meV. By contrast, for the 11 nm GaBi$_{0.017}$As$_{0.983}$/Al$_{0.142}$Ga$_{0.858}$As single quantum well (sample 2) and the triple-well structure with 6.4 nm GaBi$_{0.022}$As$_{0.978}$/Al$_{0.137}$Ga$_{0.863}$As wells (sample 4), the hh1-lh1 splitting is reproduced within 1-2 meV of the measured values.

The constrained 12-band model reproduces the measured transition energies across additional QWs beyond those used to fit the parameters: for the wide 11 nm single QW (sample 2) the calculated transition energies match the measured values very well (e.g., $e1$–hh1 and $e1$–lh1 within $\sim1\ \text{meV}$), demonstrating accurate description of wide wells; for the triple-well structure (sample 4) good agreement is obtained by modest adjustments of nominal QW width and Bi composition within growth uncertainty ranges, reproducing the measured hh1–lh1 splitting (calculated 45.5 meV vs measured 47 meV), and for the GaAs-barrier sample (sample 6) the calculated $e1$–hh1 transition matches the measured value, with the calculated small CB offset ($31\ \text{meV}$) consistent with experimental observation. 
        Fig. 3(c)-4(f)
        Table 4

Quantitatively, the overall agreement between measured and calculated transition energies for samples 3–6 using the constrained parameter set is good: the calculated energies listed in the results table (Table 4) lie close to the measured energies for the $e1$–hh1 and $e1$–lh1 transitions in each structure, showing that the fitted parameters are transferable across changes in well width, Bi composition (within the studied range around $\sim 2\%$), and barrier material (AlGaAs versus GaAs). 
        Table 4

The authors acknowledge that discrepancies remain in some narrow 6.4 nm wells (samples 3,5,6) where the model overestimates the hh1–lh1 splitting by up to $\sim 10\ \text{meV}$, suggesting that compositional inhomogeneity and short-range alloy disorder—effects not explicitly modelled in the 12-band Hamiltonian—can influence the detailed valence-band structure; nevertheless, the model's ability to reproduce the main transition energies across multiple structures demonstrates practical transferability suitable for analysing QW electronic structure and guiding device design.

motivating_questions.content: The dilute-bismide Hamiltonian had to do more than fit a single calibration structure: it needed to remain predictive when the well width, Bi composition, and barrier material changed. Before this work, the practical use of the 12-band model for real GaBi$_x$As$_{1-x}$ laser structures was limited because the model parameters had not yet been tied tightly enough to experiment to establish transferability. Without that validation, the model could not be used confidently to analyse the electronic structure of other dilute-bismide quantum-well devices.

An optimization procedure was established to downfold a multiple-$\zeta$ LCAO basis (obtained from a fixed DFT density) to an optimal single-$\zeta$ minimal basis by maximizing the overlap norm
$$
N = \frac{1}{N_{\mathrm{e}}} \sum_{n} f_{n} \langle \psi_{n} | \hat{1}' | \psi_{n} \rangle,
$$
with $N_{\mathrm{e}}$ the number of electrons, KS eigenstates $|\psi_{n}\rangle$, occupations $f_n$, and
$$
\hat{1}' = \sum_{I\mu,J\nu} |\varphi_{I\mu}\rangle (S^{-1})_{I\mu,J\nu} \langle \varphi_{J\nu}|,
$$
where $|\varphi_{I\mu}\rangle$ are the single-$\zeta$ basis functions and $S_{I\mu,J\nu}=\langle\varphi_{I\mu}|\varphi_{J\nu}\rangle$. After obtaining the optimal single-$\zeta$ basis, a Löwdin orthogonalization of the Hamiltonian was performed; the resulting orthogonalized d–d intersite Hamiltonian matrix elements are effectively transferable between crystalline structures of the same nearest-neighbour distance. The intersite d–d Slater–Koster bond integrals $\beta_{\mathrm{dd}\lambda}(R)$ ($\lambda=\sigma,\pi,\delta$) are modeled by a single exponential,
$$
\beta_{\mathrm{dd}\lambda}(R) = a_{\mathrm{dd}\lambda} \exp(-b_{\mathrm{dd}\lambda} R),
$$
with fitted coefficients $a_{\mathrm{dd}\lambda}$ and $b_{\mathrm{dd}\lambda}$ extracted from orthogonalized matrix elements (dimer and crystalline data).
<problem>
In constructing a computationally efficient TB representation that retains the essential quantum-mechanical bonding of transition metals, the challenge is to choose a minimal basis that reproduces DFT wavefunctions sufficiently well while producing intersite Hamiltonian elements that are transferable across different local environments. Previously, multiple-$\zeta$ LCAO bases gave good variational flexibility but are too large for efficient TB models; naive truncation can produce non-transferable, environment-sensitive matrix elements. There was no straightforward, numerically stable recipe to (i) derive a single-$\zeta$ minimal basis from DFT LCAO data that maximizes fidelity to the KS states, (ii) orthogonalize that basis so that the two-centre approximation becomes valid and bond integrals are transferable, and (iii) parametrize a compact analytic form for bond integrals that can be used in atomistic TB simulations. Without such a procedure, TB models risked either poor reproduction of DFT electronic structure or lack of transferability between phases, preventing their reliable use in alloy studies and large-scale simulations.
</problem>

In this construction, $V_{\mathrm{T}}$ is represented by a tight-binding model for hydrocarbons, and $V_{\mathrm{I}}$ is approximated by a sum of atom-atom Buckingham, or exp/6, interactions. This analytic form had already been used successfully for methane-bath systems, but its transferability to larger hydrocarbons had not yet been established. [10,11,15,16]

The transferability test is carried out by comparing trajectory calculations on the analytic TB + exp/6 potential energy surface with direct dynamics calculations on the MP2/aug'-cc-pVDZ potential energy surface for $\mathrm{C}_{2}\mathrm{H}_{6}+\mathrm{He}$ and $\mathrm{C}_{2}\mathrm{H}_{5}+\mathrm{He}$. The quantity compared is the average deactivating energy transfer, $\langle \Delta E_{\mathrm{d}} \rangle$, which is the key low-order energy-transfer moment relevant to unimolecular kinetics. The comparison shows that the analytic TB + exp/6 results agree with the direct dynamics results typically within the statistical uncertainty of the direct calculations. The paper also notes a possible overprediction of $\langle \Delta E_{\mathrm{d}} \rangle$ by about $20\%$ for $\mathrm{C}_{2}\mathrm{H}_{5}+\mathrm{He}$, especially at low temperature. Because the agreement is generally within error bars, and because the discrepancy is limited to one case and one regime, the authors conclude that the new full-dimensional $\mathrm{C}_{x}\mathrm{H}_{y}+\mathrm{M}$ potential energy surfaces are validated for larger hydrocarbons and are suitable for efficient trajectory simulations. Earlier transferable parameterizations had been established mainly for $\mathrm{CH}_{4}+\mathrm{M}$, and it was not clear whether the same pairwise analytic representation would remain reliable when applied to larger, more flexible hydrocarbons whose interaction anisotropy and internal structure could alter the collision dynamics. An automated parameterization workflow for the Extended Hückel Molecular Orbital (EHMO) tight-binding Hamiltonian for bulk crystals was implemented that: (a) represents the total Hamiltonian as $H^{tot}=H^{eh}+H^{rep}+H^{csc}$ and fits parameters using only the extended Hückel part $H^{eh}$ where the diagonal element for atomic orbital $i$ is $H^{eh}_{ii}=-E_i$ with $E_i$ the ionic (orbital) energy, and the off-diagonal element for $i\neq j$ is
      $$
      H^{eh}_{ij}=K(R_{ij})\frac{H^{eh}_{ii}+H^{eh}_{jj}}{2}S_{ij},
      $$
      where $S_{ij}$ is the overlap integral computed from Slater-type orbitals and $K(R_{ij})$ is the modified Wolfsberg-Helmholtz factor (here taken as a distance-independent constant $K=2.3$ in all reported fits). (b) Uses double-$\zeta$ Slater-type radial functions for each $s,p,d$ valence orbital with parameters $\zeta_{1}$, $\zeta_{2}$ ($\zeta_1>\zeta_2$) and mixing ratio $\alpha=c_2/c_1$, so that each orbital is specified by four fit parameters $\{E,\zeta_1,\zeta_2,\alpha\}$. (c) Samples the Brillouin zone with 190 $k$-points and defines an objective function as the squared sum of band-energy differences between TB and first-principles bands (ABINIT) over a chosen set of bands (for example, the four or nine lowest bands). (d) Minimizes that objective function by a modified steepest-descent algorithm to produce an optimized TB parameter set for a bulk crystal. This workflow is packaged for automated execution to produce TB parameter sets that reproduce chosen first-principles band data.

      $$
      H^{eh}_{ij}=K(R_{ij})\frac{H^{eh}_{ii}+H^{eh}_{jj}}{2}S_{ij},
      $$

steps.reasoning:
Define the total electronic Hamiltonian $H^{tot}$ as the sum of three contributions: $H^{tot}=H^{eh}+H^{rep}+H^{csc}$, where $H^{eh}$ is the extended Hückel Hamiltonian, $H^{rep}$ is the repulsive Hamiltonian, and $H^{csc}$ is the charge self-consistent Hamiltonian; this decomposition is the starting formal model for the parameterization procedure.
        [1]

State the working choice for parameter determination: use only the extended Hückel Hamiltonian $H^{eh}$ to determine tight-binding parameters, treating $H^{rep}$ and $H^{csc}$ as separable contributions to be handled independently of the $H^{eh}$ fit; this reduces the fitting target to reproducing band energies from $H^{eh}$.
        [1]

Specify the diagonal and off-diagonal matrix elements of $H^{eh}$ used in the fit: for an atomic orbital labeled $i$ (where $i$ denotes an atomic orbital of type $s$, $p$, or $d$), the diagonal matrix element is $H^{eh}_{ii}=-E_i$, where $E_i$ denotes the ionic (orbital) energy; for distinct orbitals $i\neq j$, the off-diagonal element is
        $$
        H^{eh}_{ij}=K(R_{ij})\frac{H^{eh}_{ii}+H^{eh}_{jj}}{2}S_{ij},
        $$
        where $K(R_{ij})$ is the modified Wolfsberg-Helmholtz factor as a function of the interatomic distance $R_{ij}$ and $S_{ij}$ is the overlap integral between the two orbitals computed from their Slater-type radial functions.
        [4]

Adopt a specific practical choice for $K(R_{ij})$ during parameter optimization: take $K(R_{ij})$ to be a distance-independent scalar constant $K=2.3$ for the fits reported in this work, thereby fixing the empirical scalar factor and delegating variation of off-diagonal couplings to the computed overlaps $S_{ij}$ and the fitted ionic energies $E_i$.
        [5]

Define the functional form of the atomic radial orbitals used to compute overlaps $S_{ij}$: use double-$\zeta$ Slater-type orbitals (STOs) for each valence orbital ($s,p,d$) with radial component
        $$
        R_{n}(r)=\frac{r^{n-1}}{f}\left[c_1\sqrt{\frac{(2\zeta_1)^{2n+1}}{(2n)!}}e^{-\zeta_1 r}+c_2\sqrt{\frac{(2\zeta_2)^{2n+1}}{(2n)!}}e^{-\zeta_2 r}\right],
        $$
        where $n$ is the orbital quantum number ($n=1$ for $s$, $n=2$ for $p$, etc.), $c_1$ and $c_2$ are coefficients constrained by normalization with $f^2=c_1^2+c_2^2+2c_1c_2\left(\frac{4\zeta_1\zeta_2}{(\zeta_1+\zeta_2)^2}\right)^{n+\frac{1}{2}}$, and adopt the ratio $\alpha=c_2/c_1$ as an independent parameter; this establishes that each orbital is parameterized by four quantities $(E,\zeta_1,\zeta_2,\alpha)$.
        [5]

State the parameter-counting implication: for each atomic valence orbital type ($s$, $p$, $d$) there are four fit parameters — the ionic energy $E$, the two Slater exponents $\zeta_1$ and $\zeta_2$ with the constraint $\zeta_1>\zeta_2$, and the mixing ratio $\alpha$ — so that a single element with $s,p,d$ valence orbitals involves $4\times 3=12$ fit parameters in total.

Define the objective function used to compare tight-binding and first-principles bands: sample the Brillouin zone with a dense grid of $190$ $k$-points (where a $k$-point denotes a crystal wavevector in the Brillouin zone) and compute the squared-sum (sum of squared differences) between TB band energies (eigenvalues of $H^{eh}$ evaluated at each $k$-point for the chosen set of bands) and the corresponding first-principles band energies produced by ABINIT; the objective function is the sum over sampled $k$-points and over the chosen band indices of the squared band-energy differences.
        Fig. 1

Specify the choice of bands that can be targeted in the objective: the workflow supports optimizing over a chosen subset of bands (for example the four lowest bands or the nine lowest bands), such that the objective function sums differences only over those selected bands and the $190$ $k$-points; this choice controls whether the fit emphasizes only the lowest occupied/near-gap bands or a larger portion of the low-energy spectrum.

Describe the optimization algorithm: minimize the squared-sum objective by a modified steepest-descent method (the authors state they use a modified steepest descent optimizer), adjusting the orbital parameters $(E,\zeta_1,\zeta_2,\alpha)$ for each orbital to reduce the objective until convergence.
        [5]

Explain the automation and packaging: implement the entire sequence — initial guess of tight-binding parameters, computation of overlaps $S_{ij}$ from double-$\zeta$ STOs, evaluation of $H^{eh}$ and its band energies at the $190$ $k$-point grid, objective-function evaluation against ABINIT band energies, and parameter updates by the modified steepest-descent optimizer — as an automated workflow (schematically summarized in the flowchart) so that the procedure can be executed reproducibly to produce optimized TB parameter sets for bulk crystals.
        Fig. 1

motivating_questions.content: In bulk electronic-structure modeling one needs compact TB parameter sets that both capture orbital energetics and interatomic couplings with sufficient fidelity to first-principles band structures and that can be generated systematically for many elements and compounds. Previously, TB parameter choices combined empirical diagonal energies and ad hoc prescriptions for off-diagonal couplings (for example, element-dependent $K$ constants) or relied on manual tuning; double-$\zeta$ orbital forms had been proposed but not embedded in a fully automated, objective-driven bulk-fitting workflow. Without a reproducible algorithmic workflow that (i) defines a clear objective function comparing TB and first-principles bands across $k$-space, (ii) uses a compact double-$\zeta$ orbital parameterization per $s,p,d$ orbital, and (iii) employs an optimization algorithm, practitioners could not routinely generate parameter sets for bulk crystals that enable large-scale TB-based simulations while maintaining quantitative agreement with first-principles electronic structure. The automated procedure addresses this gap by prescribing the parameter set, the band-sampling, the objective function, and the optimization route needed for reproducible bulk TB parameter determination.

reasoning_chains.conclusion_text:
A local environment tight-binding Hamiltonian of the form
$$
H_{\mathrm{LETB}}=\sum_{ij\sigma} t_{ij}^{\mathrm{LETB}}\big(\vec{R}_i,\vec{R}_j,\{\vec{R}_{ij}\}\big)\,c_{i\sigma}^\dagger c_{j\sigma}+\mathrm{H.c.},
$$
where $t_{ij}^{\mathrm{LETB}}$ depends on the pair positions and the local set of nearby nuclear coordinates $\{\vec{R}_{ij}\}$, was constructed by combining the intralayer regression models (conclusion 1) and the refitted FK interlayer form (conclusion 2), and trained on a dataset of 72 distinct deformed bilayer graphene primitive-cell configurations. The model reproduces DFT/Wannierized $\pi$-band tight-binding parameters and, when applied to computed band structures, reproduces the DFT band energies of the four low-energy $\pi$ bands with very small errors; transferability to twisted geometries is demonstrated by excellent agreement between LETB and DFT bands at $9.4^\circ$ and $4.4^\circ$ twists.
reasoning_chains.conclusion_title: Local environment tight-binding (LETB) Hamiltonian trained on 72 DFT configurations and validated against DFT Wannier bands

conclusion.content:
A local environment tight-binding (LETB) Hamiltonian of the form
      $$
      H_{\mathrm{LETB}}=\sum_{ij\sigma} t_{ij}^{\mathrm{LETB}}\big(\vec{R}_i,\vec{R}_j,\{\vec{R}_{ij}\}\big)\,c_{i\sigma}^\dagger c_{j\sigma}+\mathrm{H.c.},
      $$
      where $i,j$ are atomic indices, $\sigma$ is the spin index, $c_{i\sigma}^\dagger$ creates a localized $p_z$ orbital on site $i$ with spin $\sigma$, $\vec{R}_i$ is the position of atom $i$, and $\{\vec{R}_{ij}\}$ is the set of nuclear positions in the local environment of atoms $i$ and $j$, was constructed by combining the intralayer hopping models (first-nearest-neighbor hopping linear in distance $a$, second-nearest-neighbor hopping linear in distance $b$ and hexagon-shape descriptors $h_1$, $h_2$, third-nearest-neighbor hopping linear in distance $c$ and hexagon-size descriptors $h$, $l$) with the Fang–Kaxiras interlayer hopping form (parameters $\lambda_0=239(2)$ meV, $\xi_0=2.12(2)$, $\kappa_0=1.871(4)$, $\lambda_3=-40(1)$ meV, $\xi_3=3.8(4)$, $x_3=0.52(4)$, $\lambda_6=-5.9(7)$ meV, $\xi_6=6.0(8)$, $x_6=1.52(1)$, $\kappa_6=1.73(2)$). The model was trained on a dataset of 72 distinct deformed bilayer graphene primitive-cell configurations. It reproduces DFT/Wannierized $\pi$-band tight-binding parameters and, when applied to computed band structures, reproduces the DFT band energies of the four low-energy $\pi$ bands with very small errors; transferability to twisted geometries is demonstrated by excellent agreement between LETB and DFT bands at $9.4^\circ$ and $4.4^\circ$ twists.

premises.content: The LETB Hamiltonian, trained exclusively on 72 primitive-cell bilayer configurations, was used to compute band structures of twisted bilayer graphene at $9.4^\circ$ and $4.4^\circ$ twist angles and compared against direct DFT band structures at the same twist angles (Fig. 6).  The four low-energy $\pi$ bands from LETB and DFT show negligible differences across the $K$–$\Gamma$–$M$–$K'$ path; the LETB bands lie essentially on top of the DFT bands within the linewidth of the figure.
premises.metadata: {"role": "highlight", "conclusion_id": "3", "strength_types": ["generalization"], "credit": "This validation demonstrates that the LETB model, constructed from local environment descriptors and fitted on primitive-cell deformations, successfully generalizes to twisted geometries not part of the training set.  The twisted geometries involve supercells with many atoms and non-uniform stacking patterns that differ substantially from the primitive-cell training configurations.  If the LETB had only been validated by in-sample cross-validation, the extrapolation to twisted geometries would be unverified; any claims about TBLG band structure (Conclusions 4\u20136) would depend on an assumption of transferability.  This validation directly underwrites the claim in Conclusion 3 that the model reproduces DFT band energies for twisted bilayers and provides essential confidence for applying the model to the small-twist regime."}

premises.content: The DFT calculations (using the BEEF-VDW van der Waals functional and a polarized triple-$\zeta$ all-electron basis) that produce the training data are validated against angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) for AB bilayer graphene (Fig. 12).  Near the Fermi level, the DFT and ARPES dispersions agree within $0.1$ eV, and the deviation increases away from the $K$ point but does not exceed $10\%$ of the experimental binding energy.
premises.metadata: {"role": "highlight", "conclusion_id": "3", "strength_types": ["measurement", "external"], "credit": "This external validation against experimental data shows that the DFT functional (BEEF-VDW) provides a faithful description of the $\\pi$ bands in bilayer graphene, the same electronic manifold that the LETB aims to model.  Because the LETB is trained on DFT-derived Wannier hoppings, any systematic error in DFT would be inherited by the LETB.  The ARPES comparison partially bounds these errors to the $\\sim 0.1$ eV level for low-energy bands, which is about $10$\u2013$20\\%$ of typical nearest-neighbor hopping magnitudes but much larger than the meV-scale bandwidth at the magic angle.  However, the comparison shows that DFT is quantitatively reliable for the band structure that the LETB reproduces, supporting the credibility of the LETB training data and thus the physical relevance of the LETB predictions.  Without this external check, one could argue that the LETB faithfully reproduces only the DFT (which itself might be inaccurate), but the ARPES agreement shows that the DFT is a reasonable target."}

premises.content:
The intralayer tight-binding hopping terms for first-, second-, and third-nearest neighbors are quantitatively described by linear regression models that include explicit local-environment geometric descriptors, with the following fitted forms (cross-validated parameter means and standard deviations over five folds):
      - nearest-neighbor (1-NN) intralayer hopping: $t_{1} = -9.68(4) + 2.52(1)\,a$,
      - second-nearest-neighbor (2-NN) intralayer hopping: $t_{2} = 1.55(1) + 0.022(2)\,b -0.66(1)\,h_1 -0.20(1)\,h_2$,
      - third-nearest-neighbor (3-NN) intralayer hopping: $t_{3} = -1.23(1) + 0.04(1)\,c -0.12(1)\,h + 0.23(1)\,l$.
      Here $a$, $b$, $c$ are the interatomic distances for first-, second-, and third-nearest-neighbor pairs, respectively; $h_1$ and $h_2$ are local-hexagon-shape descriptors that parametrize the shape of the hexagon formed by the six atoms surrounding the hopping centers; and $h$ and $l$ are hexagon-size descriptors that parametrize the size of the entire hexagonal environment around the hopping centers. These models were selected by least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) feature selection and fitted by five-fold cross-validated ordinary least-squares regression, and they achieve high predictive quality ($R^2$ values of 0.98 for 1-NN and 0.96 for 3-NN), demonstrating that distance-only parametrizations fail (especially for 2-NN and 3-NN) and that explicit many-atom geometric descriptors are required for quantitatively accurate intralayer hoppings.

premises.content:
The interlayer hopping is parametrized using the Fang–Kaxiras functional form
      $$
      t^{\mathrm{FK}}(\vec{r},\theta_u,\theta_d)=V_0(r_{xy}/a)+V_3(r_{xy}/a)\big[\cos(3\theta_u)+\cos(3\theta_d)\big]+V_6(r_{xy}/a)\big[\cos(6\theta_u)+\cos(6\theta_d)\big],
      $$
      with
      $V_0(r)=\lambda_0 e^{-\xi_0 r^2}\cos(\kappa_0 r),\quad
      V_3(r)=\lambda_3 r^2 e^{-\xi_3(r-x_3)^2},\quad
      V_6(r)=\lambda_6 e^{-\xi_6(r-x_6)^2}\sin(\kappa_6 r).$
      Here $r_{xy}$ is the pair distance projected onto the $x$-$y$ plane, $\theta_u$ indicates the orientation of the nearest-neighbor triangle of the upper sheet atom relative to the displacement vector, $\theta_d$ is the corresponding angle for the lower sheet atom, $a = a_0/\sqrt{3} = 1.549$ bohr. The nonlinear least-squares refit to the DFT/Wannier dataset yields cross-validated parameter means with standard deviations over five folds: $\lambda_0=239(2)\,\mathrm{meV}$, $\xi_0=2.12(2)$, $\kappa_0=1.871(4)$; $\lambda_3=-40(1)\,\mathrm{meV}$, $\xi_3=3.8(4)$, $x_3=0.52(4)$; $\lambda_6=-5.9(7)\,\mathrm{meV}$, $\xi_6=6.0(8)$, $x_6=1.52(1)$, $\kappa_6=1.73(2)$. The refitted FK model captures DFT interlayer hoppings across short, intermediate, and long projected pair distances and corrects the intermediate-distance ($\sim$7–10 bohr) deficiencies of simpler distance-only parametrizations.

steps.reasoning: Start from the upstream established results treated as known: the intralayer regression models requiring local-environment descriptors (conclusion 1) and the refitted Fang–Kaxiras interlayer functional form with DFT-fitted parameters (conclusion 2) are taken as the building blocks for the combined local environment tight-binding (LETB) Hamiltonian.

Specify the LETB Hamiltonian functional form and symbol definitions used to assemble the model: define
$
H_{\mathrm{LETB}}=\sum_{ij\sigma} t_{ij}^{\mathrm{LETB}}\big(\vec{R}_i,\vec{R}_j,\{\vec{R}_{ij}\}\big)\,c_{i\sigma}^\dagger c_{j\sigma}+\mathrm{H.c.},
$
where $i,j$ label atomic sites, $\sigma$ is spin, $c_{i\sigma}^\dagger$ creates a localized $p_z$-character orbital on site $i$ with spin $\sigma$, $\vec{R}_i$ is the position of atom $i$, and $\{\vec{R}_{ij}\}$ denotes the set of nearby nuclear coordinates that define the local environment used to evaluate the environment-dependent hopping function $t_{ij}^{\mathrm{LETB}}$. This is the general LETB Ansatz used in the paper.

Describe the classification and computation pipeline that maps a given atomic configuration to a set of hoppings: (a) for each pair $i,j$ compute the displacement vector $\vec{d}=\vec{R}_i-\vec{R}_j$, (b) classify the hopping as intralayer if $|d_z|<1\,$bohr and as interlayer otherwise, (c) if intralayer, classify neighbor order via the in-plane distance $d_{xy}=\sqrt{d_x^2+d_y^2}$ into 1-NN, 2-NN, or 3-NN if $d_{xy}$ is within $\pm5\%$ of equilibrium distances $a_0$, $\sqrt{3}a_0$, and $2a_0$ respectively, (d) for in-bound classifications (interlayer and intralayer up to 3-NN) collect all atoms within $2a_0$ of atoms $i$ and $j$ to compute the required local-environment descriptors (the $h_1,h_2,h,l$ etc.), and (e) evaluate the hopping using the fitted intralayer linear regression models for 1/2/3-NN or the refitted FK interlayer formula as appropriate; return zero for out-of-bounds intralayer hoppings.

State the training dataset and the regression/fit provenance used to construct the LETB: the intralayer linear regression coefficient sets (from LASSO selection and five-fold CV OLS fits) and the FK interlayer parameters (nonlinear least-squares refit with five-fold CV) were combined to define $t_{ij}^{\mathrm{LETB}}$; these fitted building blocks were obtained from the DFT/Wannier dataset of 72 distinct deformed bilayer primitive-cell configurations described earlier, which supply the DFT-derived hopping targets and the atomic geometries for training.
Table I
[31]

Describe model validation against DFT Wannier tight-binding parameters: compute LETB predicted hopping parameters for configurations in the dataset and compare against the DFT/Wannier tight-binding parameters; the LETB reproduces the DFT/Wannierized $\pi$-band tight-binding parameters with low errors (this is evidenced by the low RMSEs reported for intralayer fits and the good agreement of interlayer fits), indicating accurate pointwise reproduction of the Wannier TB parameters across the training set.
Fig. 4

Describe transferability validation to twisted geometries: apply the LETB to full twisted-bilayer geometries reserved for testing — specifically, compute the band structures at commensurate twist angles $9.4^\circ$ and $4.4^\circ$ using the LETB Hamiltonian constructed from the primitive-cell fitted models; compare the computed LETB band structures for the four $\pi$ bands near the Fermi level to independent DFT band structures (obtained by Wannierizing those twisted configurations). The LETB reproduces the DFT band energies at both $9.4^\circ$ and $4.4^\circ$ with excellent agreement across the Brillouin-zone $k$-path, demonstrating transferability of the primitive-cell–trained LETB to twisted geometries.
Fig. 6

Conclude: combining the intralayer regression models (conclusion 1) and the refitted FK interlayer form (conclusion 2) yields a local environment tight-binding Hamiltonian $H_{\mathrm{LETB}}$ that, when trained on the 72 DFT/Wannier primitive-cell bilayer configurations, reproduces DFT/Wannier $\pi$-band tight-binding parameters and, when applied to band-structure calculations, reproduces the DFT band energies of the four low-energy $\pi$ bands with very small errors and demonstrates transferability to twisted geometries at $9.4^\circ$ and $4.4^\circ$.

motivating_questions.content: To test whether conclusions about band flattening, band isolation, and fragile topology are robust, a compact, transferable TB model is required that (i) is faithful to ab initio Wannierized parameters across representative local geometries and (ii) can be affordably evaluated across many twisted unit cells and relaxation states. Direct DFT on large moiré cells is too expensive for broad parameter sweeps, and phenomenological TB models lack first-principles calibration. The LETB Hamiltonian provides a middle ground: an explicit local-environment-dependent TB form whose parameters are directly regressed from a DFT/Wannier dataset, enabling many-band calculations that preserve DFT accuracy at greatly reduced cost.

For a ten-atom tetrahedral tight-binding Hamiltonian built from $s$-type valence orbitals with two inequivalent through-bond transfer integrals $t_1$ and $t_2$ (on-site energy $\varepsilon$), the analytic eigenvalues are
      $$
      \varepsilon + 2t_1 - \sqrt{4t_1^2 + 6t_2^2},\quad
      \varepsilon + \sqrt{2}t_2\ (\text{threefold}),\quad
      \varepsilon + 2t_1 + \sqrt{4t_1^2 + 6t_2^2},\quad
      \varepsilon - \sqrt{2}t_2\ (\text{twofold}),\quad
      \varepsilon - 2t_1\ (\text{twofold}),
      $$
      which correspond to the $1S(a_1)$, $1P(t_1)$, $2S(a_1)$, $1D(t_2)$, and $1D(e)$ molecular levels respectively. These expressions show that an anomalous triple degeneracy among $1D(t_2)$, $1D(e)$, and $2S(a_1)$ occurs when the transfer integrals satisfy the simple relation $t_2 = \sqrt{2}\,t_1$, i.e. an inflated-tetrahedron geometry rather than a regular tetrahedron ($t_1=t_2$) is the degeneracy point.

premises.content:
An orthogonal $d$-band TB total-energy model for iron was constructed with the energy functional
      $$
      E_{\mathrm{TB}}=E_{\mathrm{bond}}+E_{\mathrm{mag}}+E_{\mathrm{rep}}+E_{\mathrm{emb}}-E_{\text{free atoms}},
      $$
      where the $d$-electron bond energy for collinear spins is
      $$
      E_{\mathrm{bond}}=\sum_{\sigma=\uparrow,\downarrow}\sum_{\substack{I\mu,J\nu\\I\neq J}}\rho_{I\mu J\nu}^{\sigma}H_{I\mu J\nu},
      $$
      the Stoner exchange (magnetic) energy is
      $$
      E_{\mathrm{mag}}=-\tfrac{1}{4}\sum_J I_J m_J^2,
      $$
      with a fixed atomic Stoner parameter $I_J = 0.76$ eV for all atoms $J$,
      the pairwise repulsive term is taken as
      $$
      E_{\mathrm{rep}}=\sum_{I\neq J} a_{\mathrm{rep}}^{IJ}\exp(-b_{\mathrm{rep}}^{IJ}R_{IJ}),
      $$
      with $a_{\mathrm{rep}}=1031$ eV and $b_{\mathrm{rep}}=3.25$ Å$^{-1}$,
      and the embedding (to approximate $s$-electron contributions) is taken as
      $$
      E_{\mathrm{emb}}=-\sum_I\Big[\sum_{J\neq I}(a_{\mathrm{emb}}^{IJ})^2\exp(-b_{\mathrm{emb}}^{IJ}R_{IJ}^2)\Big]^n,
      $$
      with $n=1/2$ (square-root second-moment approximation) by default, $a_{\mathrm{emb}}=3.70$ eV, and $b_{\mathrm{emb}}=0.23$ Å$^{-2}$.
      Here $\rho_{I\mu J\nu}^{\sigma}$ is the spin-resolved density matrix between orbitals $\mu,\nu$ on atoms $I,J$; $H_{I\mu J\nu}$ are the two-center Hamiltonian matrix elements (the $\beta$ integrals) which follow an exponential distance dependence $\beta_{dd\lambda}(R)=a_{dd\lambda}\exp(-b_{dd\lambda}R)$ with parameters $a_{dd\sigma}=-34.811$ eV, $b_{dd\sigma}=1.625$ Å$^{-1}$, $a_{dd\pi}=63.512$ eV, $b_{dd\pi}=2.014$ Å$^{-1}$, $a_{dd\delta}=-50.625$ eV, $b_{dd\delta}=2.597$ Å$^{-1}$; $m_J$ and $I_J$ are the atomic magnetic moment and Stoner parameter on atom $J$; and $R_{IJ}$ is the interatomic distance. The radial exponents $b_{\mathrm{rep}}$ and $b_{\mathrm{emb}}$ were fixed from the extracted decay rates of the $d$-$d$ overlap and the $s$-$s$ dimer matrix element, respectively, leaving only two free prefactors $a_{\mathrm{rep}}$ and $a_{\mathrm{emb}}$ to be fitted to DFT energy–volume curves. The bond integrals are also supplemented with a cutoff function using $d_{\mathrm{cut}}=0.5$ Å and $R_{\mathrm{cut}}=3.5$ Å for bond integrals, and $R_{\mathrm{cut}}=5.5$ Å for repulsive and embedding terms.
